title: Reggae: Kingston’s Gift to the World
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck trace reggae from its roots in Kingston, Jamaica. They cover the mixing of cultures in Jamaica, the predecessors mento and ska, the transistor radio and sound system culture, toasting, rock steady, and the Rastafari influence after Haile Selassie's 1966 visit. They discuss the reggae rhythm, instrumentation, and the origin of the word "reggae" (Toots and the Maytals, 1968). They also cover producers like King Tubby and dub, Joe Higgs and the Wailers, Bob Marley and Peter Tosh, Jimmy Cliff and The Harder They Come, political violence in Jamaica, Marley's shooting and One Love Concert, Marley's death, the Peter Tosh and King Tubby murders, reggae's spread to London and punk, Africa, New Zealand, hip hop, and reggaeton. The episode ends with listener mail correcting "in flagrante delicto."

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode, joke about the reggae-style clap, and state that Kingston, Jamaica is the world capital of reggae.

segments.title: Jamaica's cultural mix and the timeline of reggae
segments.summary: They discuss reggae being a fairly new genre, with 1968 often cited as its birth year, and the mix of African, European, and indigenous influences in Jamaican society.

segments.title: Mento, ska, and the transistor radio
segments.summary: Mento is described as the earliest predecessor of reggae, followed by ska in the late 1950s and early 1960s influenced by American R&B. Transistor radios let Jamaicans pick up Miami stations, and the hosts compare this borrowing to sampling in hip hop.

segments.title: Sound systems and toasting
segments.summary: Electricity spread through Jamaica, letting DJs run mobile sound systems in and around Kingston. DJs developed toasting, speaking and singing over recorded music, which led to rap. The hosts joke about DJs on reggae radio shows.

segments.title: Rock steady
segments.summary: Rock steady slowed ska down and put more focus on vocals. Examples include Ain't No Sunshine and The Upsetters' early organ-heavy sound. Rock steady directly led to reggae.

segments.title: Alpha Boys School and Sister Ignatius
segments.summary: The Alpha Boys School in Kingston, a nun-run trade school with a strong music program, produced early ska and reggae horn players. Sister Mary Ignatius Davies, a jazz fan, was a key figure.

segments.title: Rastafari and Haile Selassie's 1966 visit
segments.summary: Rastafarianism predated reggae. Haile Selassie's 1966 state visit to Jamaica, where he awarded medals to Rastafarian preachers, legitimized the movement and spread it into reggae.

segments.title: Desmond Dekker, Israelites, and Rastafari origins
segments.summary: Desmond Dekker's 1968 song The Israelites is seen as a bridge from rock steady to reggae; its lyrics reflect Rastafari ideas about Babylon. Oswald Williams (Count Ozzie) drummed on an early ska record, and Marcus Garvey's prophecy is connected to Rastafari's origin.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break and return from the break.

segments.title: Reggae instrumentation and rhythm
segments.summary: Reggae uses bass, electric guitar, percussion, organ and synth, and horns. Its distinctive four-beat rhythm emphasizes the second and fourth beats, which British bands such as The Police, The Specials, and Madness adopted.

segments.title: Reggae in Britain and themes of reggae
segments.summary: Reggae caught on in Great Britain and Ireland in the 1970s. Horns were moved away from compared to rock steady and ska. Reggae themes range from spirituality and self-determination to violence and crime, with Trenchtown noted as a low-income Kingston neighborhood, and the genre is male-dominated.

segments.title: Origin of the word reggae
segments.summary: Toots and the Maytals' 1968 song Do the Reggay is cited as the source of the term. Frederick Toots Hibbert said he replaced a derogatory word. Other theories are mentioned, and Little Roy's 1968 Reggae Soul is noted. Toots and the Maytals' 1968 hit Fifty-Four Fifty-Six is also mentioned.

segments.title: Reggae in America and dub production
segments.summary: Reggae reached American audiences only gradually; Bob Marley broke through in the 1970s. Producers such as King Tubby, Lee Scratch Perry, and Osborne Ruddock (King Tubby) pioneered dub by stripping vocals and building their own effects gear.

segments.title: Dub music and hosts' aside
segments.summary: Dub is described as electronic reggae built from cast-off recording gear, compared to Kraftwerk and Devo. Hosts discuss a possible future new wave episode.

segments.title: Joe Higgs and early Wailers
segments.summary: Joe Higgs mentored Bob Marley, Peter Tosh, and Bunny Wailer. His 1960 hit Manny-O with Higgs and Wilson sold 50,000 copies. Early Wailers songs like Simmer Down show strong R&B influence.

segments.title: Bob Marley's early life
segments.summary: Bob Marley's white Jamaican father, Norville Marley, was a plantation overseer and gave little involvement. His grandfather was a farmer and herbal healer. Marley and Bunny Wailer were raised like brothers, and they met Peter Tosh as teenagers in Trenchtown.

segments.title: Rita Marley, Catch a Fire, and early albums
segments.summary: Rita Marley visited Haile Selassie in 1966 and connected Rastafari to reggae. Catch a Fire (1972) is considered the Wailers' first full reggae album. Talking Blues is a compilation with studio talk.

segments.title: Jamaican accent aside
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the Jamaican accent and joke about accent impressions and Irn-Bru.

segments.title: Roots reggae and Peter Tosh's solo work
segments.summary: Roots reggae combines reggae music with Rastafari perspective. The Wailers broke up in 1974. Peter Tosh's albums Legalize It (1976), Equal Rights, and Nuclear Ware are discussed. Marley's lyrics are compared to Martin Luther King Jr. and Tosh's to Malcolm X. Tosh's Legalize It was banned in Jamaica, and he ran a newspaper ad with its lyrics.
topics: Martin Luther King vs Malcolm X comparison

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break before the Jimmy Cliff discussion.

segments.title: Jimmy Cliff and The Harder They Come
segments.summary: Jimmy Cliff's early hit Hurricane Hattie (1962) and his move to London are discussed. The 1972 film The Harder They Come, starring Jimmy Cliff, is described as a cult classic that spread reggae abroad, and it had a famous soundtrack.

segments.title: Gene Siskel and Roger Ebert aside
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Ebert and Siskel's reviews of The Harder They Come and mention Siskel's favorite film, Saturday Night Fever.

segments.title: Political violence and the 1976 peace concert
segments.summary: Reggae was intertwined with political violence in Jamaica. In 1976 Bob Marley played an anti-violence concert and was criticized for seeming to side with Prime Minister Michael Manley and the People's National Party. The hosts also cover the CIA claim. In 1978 the One Love Concert brought Manley and Edward Seaga together, and Marley held their hands.

segments.title: Bob Marley's shooting, death, and the murders of Peter Tosh and King Tubby
segments.summary: Marley was shot in 1976 in his home, and Rita and two others were also shot; he still played the show. He died of cancer that began on his toe and collapsed in Central Park after a Madison Square Garden show. Peter Tosh was murdered in a home invasion by Dennis Lobban. King Tubby was killed in a suspected botched robbery in 1989.

segments.title: Reggae in London and British punk
segments.summary: London became the second city of reggae after Kingston because of the Windrush generation. The Police, The Specials, and Madness were influenced by reggae, and Johnny Rotten and John Wardle of Public Image Ltd were influenced by dub.

segments.title: Reggae around the world: Africa and New Zealand
segments.summary: Reggae spread to South Africa and the Ivory Coast, and artists such as Bobi Wine in Uganda and Shatta Wale in Ghana became political leaders. Bob Marley's 1979 Auckland show sparked Maori reggae.

segments.title: Reggae's influence on hip hop and reggaeton
segments.summary: DJ Kool Herc, who was born in Kingston, brought Jamaican toasting and sound system traditions to the Bronx, which the hosts link to hip hop's origins. Reggaeton and Bad Bunny's music are described as descendants of reggae. The hosts also name their favorite reggae bands.

segments.title: Listener mail: in flagrante delicto correction
segments.summary: Dave from California corrects the phrase in the Eleanor Roosevelt episode, noting the correct term is in flagrante delicto and that Josh's coined version is 'in flagrante delicado'. The hosts discuss the meaning.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and mention how to contact the show.
